Notes: Year Established basis: earliest documented Jewish presence. Danny Syon (excavator, as cited by Wikipedia) suggests textual and archaeological evidence indicate a Jewish presence at Gamla antedating Alexander Jannaeus; a Jewish-majority civilian population likely emerged in the last quarter of the 2nd c. BCE under John Hyrcanus (c. 125-100 BCE; midpoint -112 used), possibly alongside a remaining garrison of the earlier Seleucid fort (3rd c. BCE Syrian Wars, not Jewish). No count given. Wikipedia used as pointer to Syon; original not accessed.

Presence (numismatic): about 60 percent of the coins recovered in the Gamla excavations are Jewish coins minted under Alexander Jannaeus (103-76 BCE; reign midpoint used, c.), per Danny Syon, 'Gamla - Portrait of a Rebellion', BAR 18:1 (1992). Indicates an established Hasmonean-period Jewish settlement; no population figure.

Event: Josephus, Antiquities 13.15.3 (13.393-394) - Alexander Jannaeus took 'the fortress of Gamala' and turned out Demetrius, governor of those places (parallel War 1.4.8 / 1.105). Hasmonean conquest and incorporation into the Jewish state; date c. 83-80 BCE campaign (81 BCE per modern summaries), not given by Josephus. No figure.

Presence/settlement change: Syon & Yavor (NEAEHL supplement, renewed excavations 1997-2000) - Area B ('Hasmonean quarter') yielded Early Bronze Age and 1st c. BCE remains exclusively and 'fell into disuse and was abandoned very late in the first century BCE' (c. -10). Shows Hasmonean-period Jewish occupation of part of the town and a later contraction/shift of that quarter (not abandonment of the town). No count.

Individual: Josephus, Antiquities 18.1.1 (18.4) - 'Judas, a Gaulonite, of a city whose name was Gamala', with Sadduc the Pharisee, incited revolt against the taxation (census of Quirinius, 6 CE). A named Jew from Gamala; no figure.

Presence (public building): Syon & Yavor - Area S building dating to the early 1st c. CE (c. 20 used) 'seems to be an entirely new type of Jewish public building of the Second Temple period'; it was apparently converted for use by refugees during the siege of 67 CE. Organized Jewish community; no count.

Presence (synagogue + mikveh): the Gamla synagogue (basalt, 17 x 25.5 m) 'was probably built between 23 and 41 CE' (midpoint 32, c.); a small building south of it contained a mikveh. Large communal synagogue indicates a sizeable Jewish town; no count. (Popular article by Ticia Verveer; earlier scholars dated it to the 1st c. BCE.)

Presence (synagogue, alternative dating): Zvi Uri Ma'oz (Tel Aviv 39, 2012) argued the synagogue was built around 50 CE and that the adjacent mikveh was made only in 67 CE (earlier a water cistern); Steven Fine dates it after 40 BCE. Scholarly disagreement on dating; no count.

Presence (domestic): 'Atiqot 50 (Syon & Yavor, Gamla 1997-2000) abstract - Area K yielded a private mansion, a three-level domestic residence of the 1st c. CE (midpoint 50, c.); Area S basilica identified as a Jewish public building. Indicates well-off Jewish households; no count.

Presence (ritual purity): a 1st c. CE olive-oil press with a ritual bath (mikveh) at the back, used to purify workers before oil production; a tub-shaped ritual bath at the lower side of the Hasmonean quarter; mikveh (4.5 x 4 m) by the synagogue. Ceramic scatter said to indicate 'a major city with thousands of residents' (no number). Popular site guide (BibleWalks).

Modern estimate of the pre-revolt population of Gamla: 3,000-4,000 (midpoint 3500), attributed by Wikipedia to Zeev Weiss ('Jewish Galilee in the First Century C.E.: An Archaeological View'); method not stated. Total population of a predominantly (Jewish-majority) Jewish town per the source. Josephus' figure of 9,000 inhabitants including armed rebels is called 'clearly exaggerated' by Kenneth Atkinson; Syon notes insurgents and villagers crowded in as refugees before the siege. Year = eve of revolt (c. 66).

Event: Josephus, Life 46-61 - at the outbreak of the revolt Gamala 'persevered in its allegiance to the Romans'; Philip son of Jacimus held the citadel of Gamala; the Babylonian Jews of Ecbatana (Batanaea) 'with their wives and children' retired to the citadel at Gamala when threatened by Varus. Refugee influx of Jews from Batanaea; no figure.
Event: Josephus, War 2.20.6 (2.574) - as commander in Galilee Josephus 'in Gaulanitis ... fortified Seleucia, and Sogane, and Gamala' (late 66 / early 67 CE). No figure.

Event: Josephus, Life 177, 185-186 - Joseph son of a female physician (midwife) incited many young men of Gamala to revolt from King Agrippa II, killing those who refused, including Chares, kinsman of Philip, and Jesus, brother of Justus of Tiberias; the people of Gamala asked Josephus for an armed force and workmen to raise their walls. Internal strife in the Jewish town, 66/67 CE; no figure.

Event: 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia - Agrippa sent Equiculus Modius to take the fortress but he was too weak (Life 24/114); Gamala, after initial loyalty to Rome, revolted, was fortified by Josephus and sided with the Zealots; the Romans took it on 23 Tishri (the JE gives 68 CE; Josephus' date corresponds to 67 CE) and 'killed all the inhabitants' (War 4.1.2-10). No figure.

Event (siege by Vespasian): Josephus, War 4.1.1-10 (4.1-83) - the city 'had been filled with those who had fled to it for safety'; it resisted Agrippa's siege for seven months; it fell on 22 Hyperberetaeus (Tishri), c. 9 Nov. 67 CE. 'The Romans killed only four thousand' while 'those who had thrown themselves over the cliff was found to be five thousand'; 'nor did anyone escape except two women'. Ancient death toll including refugees (9,000 total), regarded as exaggerated by modern scholars - not a resident count, so Population blank.

Presence (revolt coinage): six crude bronze coins unique to Gamla, inscribed 'For the redemption of Jerusalem the H(oly)' with a cup imitating the Jerusalem revolt shekels, attributed to local minting during the revolt (c. 66-67 CE; page title gives 70 CE), per Syon BAR 18:1 (1992). Shows an organized Jewish rebel community; no figure.

Popular figures (Aviva & Shmuel Bar-Am, Times of Israel travel feature 2013, no source given): Gamla 'was a Jewish town with a population of 5,000 farmers' (undated in the text) and at the siege its people 'numbered nearly 10,000 residents and war refugees'. Unattributed, undated popular estimate that mixes residents and refugees; Population left blank. Also says it was founded by Jannaeus c. 83-80 BCE.

Documented absence: after the Roman capture in 67 CE (Josephus: about 4,000 slaughtered, about 5,000 died fleeing down the slope; Wikipedia calls these numbers exaggerated) 'Gamla was abandoned, never to be rebuilt.' Destruction and abandonment of the Jewish town.
